mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a crown to be sensitive at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some mild sensitivity following a new crown placement is not unusual and often settles within a few weeks as the tooth and surrounding tissues adjust. However, sensitivity that develops some time after a crown was placed, or that worsens over time, is less typical and worth investigating. Night-time sensitivity specifically may point to bruxism or underlying pulp involvement. A dental professional can assess the crown to determine whether any intervention is needed.

mainEntity.name: Could teeth grinding be causing my crown to hurt at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism — the clenching and grinding of teeth during sleep — is one of the most common reasons for night-time crown discomfort. Many people are unaware they grind their teeth. Signs can include jaw stiffness or headaches upon waking, as well as sensitivity or soreness in crowned teeth. Your dentist can look for wear patterns and discuss whether a custom night guard may help protect your teeth and crown from grinding forces.

mainEntity.name: Can a crowned tooth still have nerve pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Unless the tooth has had root canal treatment, the pulp tissue — containing nerve fibres — remains inside the tooth beneath the crown. This means the tooth can still experience sensitivity to temperature, pressure, or inflammation. Even if a root canal was carried out prior to the crown being placed, some patients report a residual deep ache, which may be related to the surrounding ligament or bone rather than the tooth nerve itself.

mainEntity.name: What is pulpitis and could it explain my symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pulpitis refers to inflammation of the dental pulp — the soft inner tissue of a tooth. It can occur due to deep decay, trauma, or following extensive dental work. Symptoms often include sensitivity that is disproportionate to the stimulus, lingering discomfort after hot or cold exposure, and aching that worsens at night. Pulpitis can be reversible (where the pulp heals) or irreversible (where root canal treatment may be required). A clinical examination and X-rays help determine the appropriate management.

mainEntity.name: Should I be worried if my crown aches when I lie down?

acceptedAnswer.text: A positional ache when lying down is not uncommon and may simply reflect increased blood pressure to the area amplifying mild inflammation. However, it is sensible not to dismiss it entirely, particularly if the ache is persistent, worsening, or accompanied by other symptoms such as swelling or sensitivity to temperature. Booking a dental appointment for an assessment will help identify or rule out any underlying issue and provide peace of mind.

mainEntity.name: How long should I wait before seeing a dentist about crown sensitivity?

acceptedAnswer.text: If sensitivity is mild and has only just begun — particularly following recent crown placement — waiting one to two weeks to see whether it settles is reasonable. However, if sensitivity is worsening, is accompanied by swelling, a bad taste, or significant pain upon biting, it is worth seeking dental advice promptly rather than waiting. When in doubt, a brief consultation with your dental practice can help you decide on the most appropriate next steps.
